https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c07r.text: Figure caption, Students shelter in classroom as gunshots heard By Jonathan Head and Thanyarat Doksone ,Â Reporting from Debsirin School, Nonthaburi Â and Â Tiffanie Turnbull Published 7 August 2026 On Friday morning, as the final classes of the week were under way, panicked students began streaming out of a prestigious school just outside Bangkok. Inside, police say, a 14-year-old boy had opened fire. "I was standing in front of the teacher when she was shot," a shaken seventh grader tells the BBC, near the gates of Debsirin School in Nonthaburi. "She was talking to me when [the gunman] showed up." Still in her uniform, with her mother by her side, she explains how the shooter stalked from room to room. Authorities say he killed five teachers and injured 23 people - including fellow pupils - before turning the weapon on himself. Earlier, he had gunned down his grandparents. "I had to climb over the school fence to escape with other friends," the girl, who the BBC is not naming, continues. Her mother says the girl thought she might die. "[She said] 'I thought I'd never see you again'." Follow live: Thai teenager kills at least seven and injures more than 30 as PM calls shooting 'well prepared' Image source, Reuters Image caption, One student recounts having to climb over a fence to escape One 18-year-old student told Reuters he initially thought firecrackers were going off. "I didn't think it was a gun at first," he said. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again." Metres from the school gates, paramedics loaded the wounded into ambulances and rushed them to hospital, as milling crowds hugged and cried. Rescue worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith rushed to the scene after hearing children as young as 12 had been hurt. "I saw students who had been shot, some in the arm, some in the back, some in the chest. So I rushed to help get them to the hospital first," the 47-year-old rescue worker told Reuters news agency. One grieving teacher told the BBC his friend was among the dead. "She was my age. We went to this school together as students. Then we both became teachers at this school," the 31-year-old, who declined to give his name, said. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Authorities say the 14-year-old shot five teachers dead, and more than 30 injuries have been reported It is early days in the investigation and police haven't said anything about a motive. They believe the 9mm handgun the shooter used belonged to his grandfather. Forensic officers found the gunman's shots to be "quite accurate", with several hitting "vital spots" on victims' bodies. Others are filling some of the gaps. A teacher at the school has said the shooter was a good student - not aggressive and with good grades - and education authorities have described him as an avid gamer. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said study pressures may have played a role. "We learned that his grandmother was a teacher and she might have been strict with him. From what the police gathered from his close friend, they knew he was quite stressed about it." It is clear authorities will have many questions to answer in the coming days - many of them about what change this crime must trigger. Renewed calls for gun control reform This is Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in years - and the second at a school this year. In February, a head teacher and a female student were shot by an 18-year-old gunman during a school siege in southern Thailand. Four years ago, a 34-year-old in the eastern Nong Bua Lamphu province killed 37 people , most of them preschoolers, in a shooting and stabbing at a nursery. These crimes have resurfaced questions about gun control in the country. "This shouldn't have happened," the boyfriend of one of the killed teachers told reporters, clearly distressed and trying to hold back tears. More than seven million people are believed to own guns in the country, one of the highest rates of ownership in the world. Of those, more than one million are unlicensed owners. Image source, EPA Image caption, The shooting at Debsirin Nonthaburi School is the second in Thailand this year While there are restrictions on gun licences in Thailand, people can still acquire the weapons - legally or illegally - with relative ease. There is a thriving black market, aided by Thailand's porous land borders with four other nations. Problems with corruption and loose regulation in the police and military have seen weapons end up in the wrong hands. Prime Minister Anutin said he had tightened regulations when he was interior minister three years ago - suspending new gun permits. But gun crime remains rife, with deaths from gunshots among the highest in the region. And some in the community are calling for greater action. "An act of violence in an educational institution, which should be one of the safest places in our society, serves as a stark reminder for Thai society to seriously and systematically review gun control measures," Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut, leader of the People's Party - an opposition party - wrote in a Facebook post. Beállítom Miközben a valódi civileknek az elmúlt években sokszor néhány százezer vagy néhány millió forintért is pályázniuk kellett, hol sikerrel, hol sikertelenül, addig mellettük létrejött az álcivilek világa, az olyan szervezeteké, amelyek mögött a kormánypárthoz köthető személyek álltak, és amelyekhez ömlött a közpénz. Az Orbán-kormány ugyanis 16 év alatt egy olyan közpénz-szivattyúzó rendszert épített fel, amely lassan mindent átszőtt Magyarországon – erről beszélt Magyar Péter keddi Facebook-videójában . A miniszterelnök arról beszélt, a közpénzből támogatott civil és álcivil szervezetekhez, a Fideszhez és KDNP-hez köthető állami támogatások átláthatósága céljából hozták létre azt az interaktív térképet , amelyen bárki megnézheti, hogy a lakóhelyén ki, mire és mennyi közpénzt kapott. A térképen a 2022 és 2026 között kiosztott támogatásokat lehet látni, ez idő alatt a Bethlen Gábor Alapkezelő Zrt. (BGA) által lebonyolított programokból, valamint egyéb központi költségvetési forrásokból 20 ezer civil szervezet nagyjából 400 milliárd forint támogatásban részesült. „Szeretném nagyon világossá tenni: nem állítjuk azt, hogy minden, az adatbázisban szereplő civil szervezet visszaélt volna a támogatásokkal. Sőt, a civil szervezetek túlnyomó többsége tisztességes, fontos és nélkülözhetetlen munkát végez. Éppen miattuk kell ezt a rendszert megtisztítani” – mondta Magyar. A miniszterelnök szerint a valós munkát végző civilek mellett olyanokat is lehet találni az adatbázisban, amelyek a helyi civil munkára kapott támogatásokat „szipkázták fel, és ehelyett a helyi Fidesz-KDNP jelöltek politikai rendezvényeit szervezték”, vagy kampánykiadványokat, pártújságokat, szórólapokat adtak ki. „Ez már nem egyszerűen néhány furcsa pályázati döntés története. Ez egy teljes rendszer története. Egy olyan maffiarendszeré, amelyben az állam az egyik kezével közpénzt adott a hatalomhoz kötődő »civil« világnak, miközben a másik kezével a valódi, független civil társadalmat támadta, megbélyegezte és ellenséget csinált belőlük” – mondta. A miniszterelnök példaként a több mint 65 milliárd forintnyi támogatást kapott Batthyányi Lajos Alapítványt, az MCC 52 milliárddal támogatott alapítványát, a Lázár Jánoshoz köthető Jövő Nemzedék Földje Alapítványt és az Áder János-féle Kék Bolygó Alapítványt hozta fel, amelyek 27 illetve 24 milliárd forintnyi állami támogatást kaptak az elmúlt öt évben. Említést tett a veszprémi Kommentár Alapítványról, a Lezsák Sándorhoz köthető Népfőiskola Alapítványról és a Pócs Jánoshoz kötődő szervezetről is. „Ezek a szervezetek az országos, vagy helyi maffiacsápok, az illegális párt- és kampányfinanszírozások bizonyítékai” – mondta. Magyar Péter azt ígérte, ahol szabálytalanságot találnak, azt kivizsgálják, ahol hűtlen kezelés, tiltott pártfinanszírozás vagy más bűncselekmény gyanúja merül fel, feljelentést tesznek. Ahol pedig nincs bűncselekmény, de politikai visszaélés történt a közpénzzel, azt nyilvánosságra hozzák. „Végül a maffiatagokhoz szólnék, helyben és országosan, azokhoz, akiket gazdagítottak ezek az adófizetői milliárdok”, mondta Magyar, majd arról beszélt, tudja, hogy a közpénz nagy része már „eltűnt”, de ami még maradt, azt kérik vissza az adófizetők. „Azt javaslom, nézzék át a szervezetek bankszámláit, és a jogosulatlanul, méltánytalanul megkapott pénzeket utalják vissza, még ma” – mondta. Bos, Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief BUCHAREST/BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – Romania and neighboring Hungary are facing an energy crisis linked to a record heat wave and the related low level of the Danube River, with Romania forced to shut down its last operating nuclear reactor while Hungary struggles to keep the only one of its four Paks reactors still operating online. https://www.worthynews.com/wordpressimages/2026/08/WorthyNewsRadioAug14.mp3 Romanian authorities used controlled explosions in a desperate attempt to increase Danube water levels needed to cool the country’s Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant. But Romeo Urjan, director of the Cernavodă plant, suggested that the efforts were insufficient. “There is no issue affecting us from the standpoint of nuclear safety. But electricity generation can no longer continue with the Danube at such a low level,” he explained. Don’t rely on social media to see what matters — get the Worthy Brief by email. Romania has been forced to bring a 330-megawatt lignite-fired power plant online to help compensate for the loss of nuclear generation. Authorities are also relying on increased wind and hydropower generation, depending on available water in reservoirs, to make up for the shortfall. The situation is not much better in neighboring Hungary, where nuclear power normally provides about 40 percent of electricity generation. ONE REACTOR Only one of the four reactors at the Paks Nuclear Power Plant is currently operating as authorities struggle with exceptionally low Danube water levels. Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said authorities had begun building “a submerged river barrier” near the plant to raise the water level needed for cooling. Magyar stressed that the dam-like structure “would initially use 35,000 cubic meters of rock, followed by another 110,000 cubic meters.” He said the project “should prevent the Danube from falling below minus 90 centimeters at the nuclear plant’s cooling-water channel, eventually allowing Paks to operate at full capacity.” The simultaneous difficulties in Romania and Hungary are raising new questions about the future reliability of nuclear power in Central and Eastern Europe as heat waves and droughts become more frequent. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian Windrush scandal Home Office lifts deportation order for man, 62, who has lived in UK for 50 years Department drops efforts to return Tony Hall to Barbados, a country he left at 12 and where he has no living relatives Amelia Gentleman Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.15 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 12.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Home Office has lifted a deportation order handed to a 62-year-old man who has lived in Britain for 50 years after criticism of the department’s attempts to remove him to Barbados, a country he left as a child. The Home Office wrote to Tony Hall on Tuesday to inform him that his deportation order had been revoked. His case had been highlighted in the Guardian a day earlier. Hall had repeatedly tried to get the deportation order lifted, arguing that as the child of parents who emigrated to the Britain as part of the Windrush generation, he had the right to remain in the UK. He has no surviving relatives in Barbados and has not visited the country since arriving in London aged 12 to join his parents and five older sisters in 1976. The Home Office had previously stated that he was liable for deportation because of a 2001 conviction for conspiracy to rob and having a firearm with intent. Police stopped Hall and his co-defendants before the robbery was committed. Hall spent eight years in prison. Officials have been attempting to deport him since the end of his sentence in 2009. As a result of his precarious immigration status, he has been prohibited from working, renting somewhere to live, receiving benefits or receiving full access to NHS treatment. Hall had argued that he should not continue to be punished as a result of a crime committed 25 years ago, and for which he had served prison time. The Home Office put him on a flight to Barbados in January 2010 in an attempt to deport him to the country of his birth, but he was returned to London on the same plane, arriving the next day. Officials in Barbados appear to have been unwilling to issue him with papers to enter because of the length of time he had been in the UK. His lawyer, Naga Kandiah at MTC Solicitors, welcomed the decision but said: “The historical injustice at the heart of this case remains unresolved. For over 17 years, our client has endured fear, detention, relentless uncertainty, exclusion from work and housing, and ultimately destitution. “The Home Office may revoke a deportation order, but it cannot give our client back 17 years of his life.” Hall said the protracted period of limbo had been very difficult, and that he was relieved that he now had “the chance to live in the country I call home without fear”. The Home Office indicated that the timing of the decision to lift the deportation was coincidental. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Clive Foster, the Windrush commissioner, the independent advocate for victims and families affected by the scandal, also intervened with the Home Office, arguing that a compassionate approach should be taken in Hall’s case. Fiona Bawdon, the author of Will I Always Be British? , a recent study of people with precarious immigration status, said: “Either the government wants to do right by all of those it harmed or it doesn’t. What ministers fail to realise is that each time they treat someone in the way they treated Tony Hall, other Windrush victims – even those who’ve now had their citizenship confirmed – feel as if they could still be at risk, as if they are not really seen as British and this could be taken away from them again.” Explore more on these topics Windrush scandal Commonwealth immigration Immigration and asylum Home Office Barbados Caribbean news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Mel B ‘heartbroken’ by Windrush scandal victims’ fight for justice Windrush compensation scheme needs significant overhaul, MPs told More than half of Windrush compensation claims rejected by Home Office, report finds ‘Hurry for justice’: Windrush victims dying without redress, commissioner says Windrush scandal still a stain on society, Floella Benjamin tells Lords event ‘Clear parallels’ with Windrush as UK-born toddler denied passport UK accused of ‘stark injustice’ as woman from Montserrat refused free NHS care Windrush officials must improve after neglecting dying woman’s claim, says ombudsman ‘Forced on us’: fears for Windrush-era club as Moss Side housing plans loom Call for urgent Windrush payouts as survivors say Home Office ‘waiting for us to die’ Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland
